title: Your First Table
summary: Create a table, insert rows, and read them back in order.
intro: So far every value you selected was typed into the query itself. Real data lives in tables. In this lesson you create a table, fill it with rows, and read them back.

steps.title: CREATE TABLE and INSERT
steps.body:
A table holds rows, and every row has the same named columns. `CREATE TABLE` names the table and lists each column with its type, using the types you already know.

```sql
CREATE TABLE pets (id integer, name text, species text, born date);
```

`INSERT INTO` adds a row. List the columns, then give one value per column, in the same order, inside `VALUES`. Text goes in single quotes and dates use `DATE 'YYYY-MM-DD'`. PostgreSQL lets you leave the column list out, but naming the columns keeps each value in the right column even if you misremember the table's order.

```sql
INSERT INTO pets (id, name, species, born) VALUES (1, 'Biscuit', 'dog', DATE '2021-04-12');
```

`SELECT * FROM pets;` reads every row. The `*` means all columns, in the order the table defines them.

Statements that change things print a command tag instead of a table. `CREATE TABLE` prints `CREATE TABLE`. An insert prints `INSERT 0 1`: the `0` is a leftover from older versions and is always 0, and the last number counts the rows added.

Every run starts from an empty database, so your program creates its own table. Creating a table that already exists is an error. Run the `CREATE TABLE` line twice in the editor to see it:

```text
ERROR:  relation "pets" already exists
```

example.title: One pet
example.prompt: Create a pets table, add one pet, and read the table back.
example.output:
CREATE TABLE

INSERT 0 1

 id |  name   | species |    born
----+---------+---------+------------
  1 | Biscuit | dog     | 2021-04-12
(1 row)
example.explanation: `CREATE TABLE` defines four columns and prints its tag. The `INSERT` lists the same four columns and matching values, so it adds one row and prints `INSERT 0 1`. `SELECT *` then prints the whole table: a header with every column name, the dashed line, the one row, and `(1 row)`.

practice.title: One book
practice.prompt:
Create a books table, add one book, and read it back.

1. Create a table named `books` with the columns `id` (integer), `title` (text), `author` (text), and `pages` (integer), in that order.
2. Insert one book: id 1, title `Dune`, author `Frank Herbert`, 412 pages.
3. Select every column of every row from `books`.

Expected output:

```text
CREATE TABLE

INSERT 0 1

 id | title |    author     | pages
----+-------+---------------+-------
  1 | Dune  | Frank Herbert |   412
(1 row)
```

hints: Follow the pets example: one `CREATE TABLE`, one `INSERT`, one `SELECT *`, each ending with a semicolon.
Text values need single quotes, like `'Dune'`. Numbers like `412` do not.

steps.title: Many rows at once
steps.body:
One `INSERT` can add many rows. Put each row in its own parentheses and separate the rows with commas. The tag counts them, so four rows print `INSERT 0 4`. A statement can span several lines, because only the semicolon ends it.

```sql
INSERT INTO scores (id, player, points)
VALUES
    (1, 'Mara', 980),
    (2, 'Theo', 760);
```

Every row needs one value per listed column. If one row is short, PostgreSQL rejects the whole statement and adds nothing. Delete a value from one row in the editor to see the error:

```text
ERROR:  VALUES lists must all be the same length
```

A table has no built-in order. `SELECT * FROM scores;` often returns rows in the order you inserted them, but PostgreSQL does not promise that, and the order can change once rows are updated or deleted. Add `ORDER BY id` to sort by the `id` column, smallest first, so the order is guaranteed:

```sql
SELECT * FROM scores ORDER BY id;
```

From here on, every query that returns more than one row ends with `ORDER BY` on a column whose values never repeat, such as `id`.

example.title: Game scores
example.prompt: Create a scores table, add four players in one statement, and read them back sorted by id.
example.output:
CREATE TABLE

INSERT 0 4

 id | player | points
----+--------+--------
  1 | Mara   |    980
  2 | Theo   |    760
  3 | Kai    |   1250
  4 | Ines   |   1430
(4 rows)
example.explanation: The four rows go in with a single `INSERT`, so the tag is `INSERT 0 4`. They were inserted out of order (3, 1, 4, 2), and `ORDER BY id` sorts them to 1, 2, 3, 4 no matter how PostgreSQL stored them. Notice how `psql` right-aligns the numbers in `points` and left-aligns the text in `player`.

practice.title: City table
practice.prompt:
Create a cities table, add four cities in one statement, and read them back sorted by id.

1. Create a table named `cities` with the columns `id` (integer), `name` (text), `country` (text), and `population` (integer), in that order.
2. In one `INSERT`, add these cities in this order: Nairobi (id 3, Kenya, 4397073), Lisbon (id 1, Portugal, 545923), Lima (id 4, Peru, 9751717), and Oslo (id 2, Norway, 709037).
3. Select every column of every city, sorted by `id`.

Expected output:

```text
CREATE TABLE

INSERT 0 4

 id |  name   | country  | population
----+---------+----------+------------
  1 | Lisbon  | Portugal |     545923
  2 | Oslo    | Norway   |     709037
  3 | Nairobi | Kenya    |    4397073
  4 | Lima    | Peru     |    9751717
(4 rows)
```

End the query with `ORDER BY id` so the rows come out as 1, 2, 3, 4.

recap:
- `CREATE TABLE name (column type, ...);` makes a table and prints `CREATE TABLE`.
- `INSERT INTO name (columns) VALUES (...);` adds a row. List several rows separated by commas to add them all at once.
- The insert tag `INSERT 0 n` reports how many rows were added.
- `SELECT * FROM name;` reads every column of every row.
- A table has no built-in order, so sort with `ORDER BY id` whenever a result has more than one row.
